column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 26: “Every joint owes a charity”

column2: From Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Every joint (sulāmā) of people owes a charity on every day on which the sun rises. Judging justly between two people is a charity;

helping a man with his mount, lifting him onto it or lifting his goods onto it for him, is a charity; a good word is a charity; every step you take towards the prayer is a charity; and removing harm from the road is a charity.”
Al-Bukhārī and Muslim reported it.
Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded this hadith through the narration of Hammām ibn Munabbih, from Abū Hurayrah.

Al-Bazzār recorded it through the narration of Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “A human being has three hundred and sixty bones” — or “thirty-six joints” — “and every day he owes a charity [for them].” They said: And whoever cannot find [the means]?
He said: “He enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong.” They said: And whoever is unable to?
He said: “He lifts a bone off the road.” They said: And whoever is unable to?
He said: “Then let him help someone weak.” They said: And whoever is unable to do that?
He said: “Then let him leave people safe from his evil.”

Muslim recorded, from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The son of Ādam was created with three hundred and sixty joints. Whoever remembers Allah, praises Allah, declares Allah's oneness and glorifies Allah,

moves a stone, a thorn or a bone out of the Muslims' path, or enjoins what is right or forbids what is wrong, to the number of those three hundred and sixty joints, reaches the evening of that day having moved himself away from the Fire.”
Muslim also recorded, through the narration of Abū al-Aswad al-Dīlī, from Abū Dharr, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every morning a charity is due on every joint of each of you.

Every tasbīḥah [subḥān Allāh] is a charity, every taḥmīdah [al-ḥamdu lillāh] is a charity, every tahlīlah [lā ilāha illā Allāh] is a charity, every takbīrah [Allāhu akbar] is a charity, enjoining what is right is a charity and forbidding what is wrong is a charity; and two rakʿahs that one prays in the forenoon (ḍuḥā) suffice for all of that.”

Imam Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Buraydah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “In a human being there are three hundred and sixty joints, and he must give a charity for each joint of his.” They said: And who can manage that, Prophet of Allah?
He said: “Phlegm in the mosque that you bury, or something you move off the road; and if you cannot find [that], the two rakʿahs of the forenoon will suffice you.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Mūsā, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every Muslim owes a charity.” They said: And if he cannot find [anything]?
He said: “Then let him work with his hands, benefit himself and give charity.” They said: And if he is unable, or does not do it?
He said: “He helps someone in need who is in distress.” They said: And if he does not do it?
He said: “Then let him enjoin good” — or he said: “what is right.” They said: And if he does not do it?
He said: “Then let him refrain from evil, for that is a charity for him.”
Ibn Ḥibbān recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“On every joint (mansim) of the son of Ādam there is a charity every day.” A man among the people said: And who can manage this?
He said: “Enjoining what is right is a charity, forbidding what is wrong is a charity, carrying [loads] for the weak is a charity, and every step one of you takes towards the prayer is a charity.”
Al-Bazzār and others recorded it.
In one narration: “On every mīsam of a human being there is a charity every day” — or “a prayer.” A man said: This is one of the hardest things you have brought us. He said:

“Enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is a prayer” — or “a charity” — “your carrying [loads] for the weak is a prayer, your removing filth from the road is a prayer, and every step you take towards the prayer is a prayer.”
In al-Bazzār's narration: “and removing harm from the road is a charity” — or he said: “a prayer.”
Someone said: By mīsam he means each limb on its own. The word is taken from wasm, a mark, since there is no bone, vein or sinew but bears the mark of Allah's handiwork.
The servant must therefore thank Allah for that and praise Him for creating him well-formed and sound, and this is what is meant by his words, “there is a prayer due from him every day”;
for prayer contains praise, thanks and extolling.

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, by another route from Ibn ʿAbbās, who raised the hadith to the Prophet ﷺ: “On every joint” — or “on every limb” — “of the children of Ādam there is a charity every day, and the two rakʿahs of the forenoon suffice for that.”
It is narrated, from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every soul owes a charity every day.” Someone said: And if he finds nothing?
He said: “Is he not sighted, vigorous, articulate and healthy?”
He said: Yes. He said: “He gives from his little and from his much. Your seeing for one whose sight is impaired is a charity, and your hearing for one whose hearing is impaired is a charity.”
In explaining the previous hadith, the hadith of Abū Dharr, we mentioned what Ibn Ḥibbān recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ: that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“There is no soul of the son of Ādam but owes a charity on every day on which the sun rises.” He was asked: Messenger of Allah, where are we to find a charity to give?
He said: “The doors of good are many: tasbīḥ, taḥmīd, takbīr and tahlīl; enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong; removing harm from the road; making the deaf hear; guiding the blind;

directing one who seeks his need to it; hurrying on your two legs with one in distress who is calling for help; and carrying with the strength of your two arms along with the weak. All of this is charity from you to yourself.”
His words ﷺ: “Every joint (sulāmā) of people owes a charity.”
Abū ʿUbayd said: The sulāmā is originally a bone in the camel's foot (firsin). He said: So the meaning of the hadith is, as it were: on every one of the bones of the son of Ādam there is a charity.
Abū ʿUbayd is indicating that sulāmā is the name of certain small bones in camels, and that it was then used for bones in general, in human beings and others.
So in his view the meaning of the hadith is: on every one of the bones of the son of Ādam there is a charity.
Others said: The sulāmā is a bone at the extremity of the hand and the foot, and it stands by metonymy for all the bones of the body. Sulāmā is a plural; it has also been said to be a singular.
The physicians have mentioned that all the bones of the body number two hundred and forty-eight, besides the sesamoid bones (sumsumāniyyāt). Some of them say they are three hundred and sixty bones,

of which two hundred and sixty-five can be perceived by the senses, while the rest are small and invisible and are called sesamoid. These hadiths confirm this view, and perhaps sulāmā is used for these small bones,
just as it is originally the name of the smallest bones in a camel. Al-Bazzār's narration of the hadith of Abū Hurayrah supports this, for in it he says:
“or thirty-six joints.” Others besides al-Bazzār recorded it with the words: “In the son of Ādam there are six hundred and sixty bones,” but this narration is a mistake.
In the hadiths of ʿĀʾishah and Buraydah, three hundred and sixty joints (mafṣil) are mentioned.

The meaning of the hadith is that the assembling of these bones and their soundness are among the greatest of Allah's blessings upon His servant. Each one of them therefore needs a charity that the son of Ādam gives on its behalf, as thanks for this blessing.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: “O mankind, what has deceived you about your Lord, the Most Generous, who created you, proportioned you and balanced you, and assembled you in whatever form He willed?” [al-Infiṭār 82:6–8]. He, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

“Say: It is He who brought you into being and gave you hearing, sight and hearts; little do you give thanks” [al-Mulk 67:23]. He also says: “Allah brought you out of your mothers' wombs knowing nothing, and gave you hearing, sight and hearts so that you might give thanks” [al-Naḥl 16:78].

And He says: “Have We not given him two eyes, a tongue and two lips?” [al-Balad 90:8–9]. Mujāhid said: These are successive blessings from Allah, which He makes you acknowledge so that you may give thanks.
Al-Fuḍayl recited this verse one night and wept. When he was asked why he was weeping, he said: Have you ever spent a night thankful to Allah for giving you two eyes with which you see?
Have you ever spent a night thankful to Allah for giving you a tongue with which you speak?
And he went on listing things of this kind.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā reported, with his chain of narration, from Salmān al-Fārisī, who said: A man had been given an abundance of this world, and then what he had was taken from him; yet he went on praising Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and extolling Him,

until he had no bedding but a reed mat (būrī), and still he went on praising Allah and extolling Him. Another man had been given an abundance of this world, and he said to the man with the reed mat: Tell me, what is it that you praise Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for?
He said: I praise Allah for things that I would not give up even if I were offered, in exchange for them, all that people have been given. He said: And what are they?
He said: What of your sight? What of your tongue? What of your hands? What of your feet?
With his chain, from Abū al-Dardāʾ, that he used to say: Health is the wealth of the body.

From Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd: A man complained to him of his straitened circumstances, and Yūnus said to him: Would it please you to have a hundred thousand dirhams in exchange for this sight of yours with which you see?
The man said: No. He said: Then a hundred thousand dirhams for your hand?
He said: No. He said: Then for your feet?
He said: No. The narrator said: Then he reminded him of Allah's blessings upon him, and Yūnus said: I see that you have hundreds of thousands, and yet you complain of need.
From Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: It is written in the wisdom of the family of Dāwūd: Well-being is a hidden kingdom.
From Bakr al-Muzanī, who said: Son of Ādam, if you want to know the extent of what Allah has blessed you with, close your eyes.
In one of the reports: How many a blessing of Allah lies in a vein that is still!
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet ﷺ said: “There are two blessings in which many people are cheated: health and free time.”

So on the Day of Resurrection a person will be asked whether he gave thanks for these blessings, and will be called to account for them, as the Exalted says: “Then you will surely be asked that Day about the blessings” [al-Takāthur 102:8].

Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Ḥibbān recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The first of the blessings the servant will be asked about on the Day of Resurrection is that He will say to him: Did We not give you a healthy body, and quench your thirst with cold water?”
Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The blessings are security and health.
It has also been narrated from him as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ).

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words, “Then you will surely be asked that Day about the blessings”: The blessings are the health of bodies, of hearing and of sight. Allah will ask
His servants what they used them for,
though He knows that better than they do. This is the sense of His words, Exalted is He: “Indeed hearing, sight and the heart — about all of these one will be questioned” [al-Isrāʾ 17:36].
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, through the narration of Ayyūb ibn ʿUtbah — and there is weakness in him — from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet ﷺ:

“Whoever says lā ilāha illā Allāh will have a covenant with Allah by it, and whoever says subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdihi, a hundred thousand and twenty-four thousand good deeds will be written for him by it.” A man said: How can we perish after this, Messenger of Allah?

He said: “A man will come on the Day of Resurrection with deeds which, if they were placed on a mountain, would weigh it down. Then one of the blessings of Allah will stand up and almost use it all up, unless Allah bestows His mercy abundantly.”
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā reported, with a chain that also contains weakness, from Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The blessings will be brought on the Day of Resurrection,
along with the good deeds and the bad deeds, and Allah will say to one of His blessings: Take your due from his good deeds. And it will leave him no good deed without taking it away.”

With his chain, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: A worshipper worshipped Allah for fifty years. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him: I have forgiven you. He said: My Lord, what is there for You to forgive me, when I have committed no sin?

So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, gave leave to a vein in his neck, and it throbbed painfully, so that he could neither sleep nor pray. Then it settled down and he stood [in prayer], and an angel came to him,
and he complained to him of the throbbing of the vein that he had suffered. The angel said: Your Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, says: Your worship of fifty years equals the stillness of that vein.
Al-Ḥākim recorded this meaning as marfūʿ, through the narration of Sulaymān ibn Haram al-Qurashī, from Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jābir, from the Prophet ﷺ:

that Jibrīl told him that a worshipper worshipped Allah on the top of a mountain in the sea for five hundred years, and then asked his Lord to take his soul while he was prostrating. He said: We pass by him whenever we descend and whenever we ascend, and we find in [Allah's] knowledge that he will be raised up on the Day of Resurrection

and made to stand before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, will say: Admit My servant into Paradise by My mercy. The servant will say: My Lord, by my deeds — three times. Then Allah will say to the angels: Weigh My servant against My blessing upon him and against his deeds.

They will find that the blessing of sight alone has taken up the worship of five hundred years, while the blessings of the body are still owed by him. He will say: Put My servant into the Fire. He will be dragged towards the Fire and will call out to his Lord: By Your mercy admit me into Paradise, by Your mercy! So He will admit him into Paradise. Jibrīl said: All things are only by the mercy of Allah, Muḥammad.
As for Sulaymān ibn Haram, al-ʿUqaylī said: He is unknown, and his hadith is not preserved (ghayr maḥfūẓ).

Al-Kharāʾiṭī reported, with a chain open to question, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr as marfūʿ: “The servant will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and made to stand before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and He will say to the angels: Look into My servant's deeds and My blessing upon him. They will look and say:

Not even the measure of a single one of Your blessings upon him. He will say: Look into his deeds, the bad and the good. They will look and find them evenly balanced. He will say: My servant, I have accepted your good deeds and forgiven your bad deeds, and I have made you a gift of My blessings in all that lies between.”

The point is that Allah the Exalted has blessed His servants with more than they can count, as He said: “If you were to count the blessings of Allah, you could not number them” [Ibrāhīm 14:34; al-Naḥl 16:18]; and He has asked them for thanks, and is pleased with it from them.

Sulaymān al-Taymī said: Allah has blessed His servants according to His measure and charged them with thanks according to theirs, so that, by way of thanks, He is pleased with them when they acknowledge His blessings in their hearts and praise Him for them with their tongues. Thus Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn Ghannām,
that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever says in the morning: ‘O Allah, whatever blessing has come to me this morning, or to any of Your creation,

is from You alone, without partner; so Yours is the praise and Yours is the thanks,’ has fulfilled the thanks due for that day; and whoever says it in the evening has fulfilled the thanks due for his night.”
In a narration of al-Nasāʾī's it is from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās.
Al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah does not bless a servant with a blessing,

and he knows that it is from Allah, but Allah writes for him the thanks for it before he gives thanks for it; and no servant commits a sin and then regrets it but Allah writes forgiveness for him before he asks for forgiveness.”

Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī said: On the day of the Mount (al-Ṭūr), Mūsā (peace be upon him) said: My Lord, if I pray, it is from You; if I give charity, it is from You; and if I convey Your message, it is from You. So how can I thank You?
He said: Now you have thanked Me.
From al-Ḥasan, who said: Mūsā (peace be upon him) said: My Lord, how can Ādam fulfil the thanks for what You did for him?

You created him with Your hand, breathed into him of Your spirit, made him dwell in Your Paradise, and commanded the angels, and they prostrated to him. He said: Mūsā, he knew that this was from Me and praised Me for it, and that was thanks for what I had done.
From Abū al-Jald, who said: I read in the supplications of Dāwūd that he said: My Lord, how can I thank You, when I can only attain to thanking You through Your blessing?
He said: Then the revelation came to him: Dāwūd, do you not know that the blessings you have are from Me?
He said: Certainly, my Lord. He said: Then I accept that from you as thanks.
He said: And I read in the supplications of Mūsā: My Lord, how can I thank You, when the smallest of the blessings You have bestowed on me cannot be repaid by all my deeds?
He said: Then the revelation came to him: Mūsā, now you have thanked Me.
Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbdullāh said: No servant ever says al-ḥamdu lillāh once without his saying al-ḥamdu lillāh placing him in debt for a further blessing. And what is the recompense for that blessing?
Its recompense is that he says al-ḥamdu lillāh; and then another blessing has come. So the blessings of Allah never run out.
Ibn Mājah reported, from the hadith of Anas as marfūʿ: “Allah does not bless a servant with a blessing, and he says al-ḥamdu lillāh, but what he gave is better than what he took.”
We have narrated something similar from the hadith of Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Asmāʾ bint Yazīd, also as marfūʿ.
This has also been narrated from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī as his own words.
One of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz's governors wrote to him: I am in a land where blessings have become so plentiful that I fear for its people that their thanks will fall short. ʿUmar wrote back to him:
I used to think you knew Allah better than you do. Allah has not blessed a servant with a blessing, and he praised Allah for it, without his praise being better than His blessings;

and you would know this even if you had nothing but the revealed Book of Allah. Allah the Exalted says: “We gave Dāwūd and Sulaymān knowledge, and they said: Praise be to Allah, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants” [al-Naml 27:15].

The Exalted also says: “Those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups, until, when they reach it…” up to His words: “And they will say: Praise be to Allah” [al-Zumar 39:73–74]. And what blessing is better than entering Paradise?
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā mentioned in Kitāb al-Shukr (“The Book of Thanks”), from one of the scholars, that he judged this view correct — I mean the view of whoever said

that praise is better than the blessings — and, from Ibn ʿUyaynah, that he judged whoever said it to be mistaken. He said: The servant's act cannot be better than the act of the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic.

But the correct view is that of the one who judged it correct. What is meant by the blessings here is the worldly blessings, such as well-being, provision and health, the warding off of what is disliked, and so on, whereas praise is one of the religious blessings.
Both are a blessing from Allah; but Allah's blessing upon His servant in guiding him to thank Him for His blessings by praising Him for them is better than His worldly blessings upon His servant.
For worldly blessings, if thanks is not joined to them, are an affliction, as Abū Ḥāzim said: Every blessing that does not bring one closer to Allah is an affliction.

So when Allah grants His servant success in thanking Him for His worldly blessings, by praise or by some other kind of thanks, this blessing is better than those blessings and more beloved to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, than they are.
For Allah loves praises, and He is pleased with His servant when he eats a mouthful and praises Him for it, and drinks a draught and praises Him for it.

To the generous and the noble, being extolled for their favours, and praised and thanked for them, is dearer than their wealth; they give their wealth away in pursuit of praise. And Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is the Most Generous of the generous and the most bountiful of the bountiful;

so He bestows His blessings on His servants and asks them to extol Him for them, to mention them and to praise Him for them, and He is pleased with that from them as thanks for them, even though all of that is from His bounty to them,
and He has no need of their thanks. Yet He loves this from His servants, since the servant's righteousness, success and perfection lie in it.

It is part of His bounty that He attributes praise and thanks to them, even though it is one of His greatest blessings upon them. In the same way He gave them the wealth He gave them and then asked them to lend Him some of it,

and praised them for giving it, though all of it is His property and from His bounty; but His generosity required that. From here the meaning can be known of the report that has come both as marfūʿ and as mawqūf (stopping short of the Prophet ﷺ): “Praise be to Allah, a praise that matches His blessings and is equal to His increase.”
Let us now return to the explanation of the hadith: “Every joint of people owes a charity on every day on which the sun rises.”
This means that the charity is due from the son of Ādam for these limbs on every one of the days of this world; for “day” is sometimes used of a period longer than that,
as when one says “the Day of Ṣiffīn”, which lasted several days, and of time in general, as in His words: “Indeed, on the Day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them” [Hūd 11:8].

It may also include both night and day. So when it is said, “every day on which the sun rises”, it is understood that this charity is due from the son of Ādam on every day he lives of the days of this world.
The apparent sense of the hadith indicates that this thanks, by means of this charity, is obligatory on the Muslim every day. But thanks is of two degrees.

The first is obligatory: that one does the obligatory duties and avoids the forbidden things. This is indispensable, and it suffices as thanks for these blessings. This is shown by what Abū Dāwūd recorded from the hadith of Abū al-Aswad al-Dīlī,
who said: We were with Abū Dharr, and he said: Every morning a charity is due on every joint of each of you, every day. He has a charity for every prayer;
fasting is a charity, Ḥajj is a charity, tasbīḥ is a charity, takbīr is a charity and taḥmīd is a charity. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ listed [several] of these righteous deeds and said:

“Two rakʿahs of the forenoon suffice each of you for all of that.” It has already been mentioned, in the hadith of Abū Mūsā recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs: “And if he does not do it, then let him refrain from evil, for that is a charity for him.”

This shows that it is enough for him not to do any evil. Yet he only avoids evil when he carries out the obligatory duties and avoids the forbidden things, for the greatest evil is to abandon the obligatory duties. Hence one of the Salaf said: Thanks is the abandoning of sins.
Another said: Thanks is that none of the blessings be used as a help to disobedience.
Abū Ḥāzim the ascetic spoke of the thanks of all the limbs: that they be held back from sins and used in acts of obedience. Then he said: As for one who gives thanks with his tongue
but does not give thanks with all his limbs, his likeness is that of a man who has a cloak and takes hold of its edge without putting it on; that does not protect him from heat, cold, snow or rain.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: Let the servant consider Allah's blessings upon him in his body, his hearing, his sight, his hands, his feet and so on. There is nothing of this but contains a blessing from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
The servant is duty-bound to use the blessings in his body for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in obeying Him. Another blessing lies in provision;
he is duty-bound to act for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in obeying Him with the provision He has bestowed on him. Whoever does this has taken the sure course of thanks, its root and its branch.
Al-Ḥasan saw a man strutting as he walked, and said: Allah has a blessing in every limb of his. O Allah, do not make us among those who use Your blessings to gain strength for disobeying You.

The second degree of thanks is recommended thanks: that the servant, after fulfilling the obligatory duties and avoiding the forbidden things, does voluntary acts of obedience. This is the degree of the foremost, those brought near, and it is what the Prophet ﷺ directed people to in the hadiths mentioned above.

So too the Prophet ﷺ used to strive hard in prayer, standing until his feet were swollen and cracked; and when it was said to him: Do you do this, when Allah has forgiven you your past and future sins?
he would reply: “Should I not be a thankful servant?”
One of the Salaf said: When Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said, “Work, family of Dāwūd, in thanks” [Sabaʾ 34:13], no hour of night or day passed over them without someone among them praying.

This is so even though some of the deeds the Prophet ﷺ mentioned are obligatory: either on each individual, such as walking to the prayer, according to those who hold that praying in congregation in the mosques is obligatory,

or as a communal obligation, such as enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, coming to the aid of one in distress, and justice between people, whether in judging between them or in reconciling them.
It has been narrated, from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The best charity is setting things right between people.”

Of the kinds of charity the Prophet ﷺ pointed to, some have a benefit that extends to others, such as reconciling people; helping a man with his mount, lifting him onto it or lifting his goods onto it; and the good word,

which includes the greeting of peace and blessing one who sneezes; removing harm from the road; enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong; burying phlegm in the mosque; helping someone in need who is in distress; making the deaf hear; seeing for one whose sight is impaired; and guiding the blind, or anyone else, on the way.

In some narrations of the hadith of Abū Dharr: “and your speaking for one who cannot speak (al-artam) is a charity,” meaning one who is unable to speak, whether because of a defect in his tongue or because his speech is foreign, so that you explain on his behalf what needs explaining.

Others have a benefit confined to the one who does them, such as tasbīḥ, takbīr, taḥmīd and tahlīl, walking to the prayer, and praying the two rakʿahs of the forenoon. These two rakʿahs suffice for all of that only
because in prayer all the limbs are used in obedience and worship, so it suffices as thanks for the blessing of the soundness of these limbs.

Most of the other traits mentioned involve the use of only some of the body's limbs, so the charity is not complete through them until one does as many of them as there are joints in the body, which are three hundred and sixty, as in the hadith of ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her).
In the Musnad, from Ibn Masʿūd, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Do you know which charity is best and finest?”
They said: Allah and His Messenger know best.
He said: “The minḥah: that you lend your brother dirhams, or the back of a mount, or the milk of a sheep or the milk of a cow.”

What is meant by the minḥah of dirhams is lending them; by the minḥah of a mount's back, ifqār, which is lending it to someone to ride; and by the minḥah of the milk of a sheep or a cow, that he gives him a cow or a sheep to drink its milk and then return it to him. When manīḥah is used without qualification, it refers only to this last.
Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever gives a manīḥah of milk or of silver, or guides someone along a lane (zuqāq),

will have the like of freeing a slave.” Al-Tirmidhī said: His words, “Whoever gives a manīḥah of silver”, mean only the lending of dirhams, and his words, “or guides someone along a lane”, mean only guiding on the road, that is, showing the way.
Al-Bukhārī recorded, from the hadith of Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah, from Abū Kabshah al-Salūlī, who said: I heard ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr say: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“There are forty traits, the highest of which is lending a she-goat [for its milk]. No one acts on one of them, hoping for its reward and believing in what is promised for it, but Allah admits him into Paradise by it.”
Ḥassān said: We counted the traits below lending a she-goat — returning the greeting, blessing one who sneezes, removing harm from the road and the like — and we could not reach fifteen.

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Jābir, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The due on camels is milking them at the watering place, lending their bucket, lending their stud, lending them out [for their milk], and giving a mount on them in the path of Allah.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Jābir, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every good deed (maʿrūf) is a charity. It is a good deed to meet your brother with a cheerful face, and to pour from your bucket into his vessel.”

Al-Ḥākim and others recorded it with an addition: “Whatever a person spends on himself and his family is written for him as a charity; whatever he protects his honour with is written for him as a charity; and for every expenditure a believer makes, Allah stands surety for its replacement, except spending on sin or on building.”

In the Musnad, from Abū Jurayy al-Hujaymī, who said: I asked the Prophet ﷺ about doing good, and he said: “Do not belittle any good deed, even if it is giving a piece of rope, even if it is giving a sandal strap,

even if it is pouring from your bucket into the vessel of one seeking water, even if it is moving something from people's path that harms them, even if it is meeting your brother with your face cheerful towards him, even if it is meeting your brother and greeting him with peace, and even if it is keeping company with the lonely in the land.”
Among the kinds of charity is withholding harm from people, with the hand and the tongue, as in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from Abū Dharr: I said: Messenger of Allah, which deeds are best?
He said: “Faith in Allah and jihād in His path.” I said: And if I do not do [that]?
He said: “Help a craftsman, or make something for one who is unskilled.” I said: Tell me, what if I am too weak for some of the work?
He said: “Withhold your evil from people, for that is a charity.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān, from Abū Dharr, who said: I said: Messenger of Allah, direct me to a deed that will take the servant into Paradise if he does it. He said: “He believes in Allah.” I said:
Messenger of Allah, surely there is a deed to go with faith?
He said: “He gives a little of what Allah has provided him.” I said: And if he is destitute and has nothing?
He said: “He says something good with his tongue.” I said: And if he is inarticulate and his tongue cannot speak for him?
He said: “Then he helps one who is overpowered.” I said: And if he is weak and has no strength?
He said: “Then let him make something for one who is unskilled.” I said: And if he is himself unskilled?
He turned to me and said: “Do you not want to leave any good at all in your companion?

Let him leave people safe from his harm.” I said: Messenger of Allah, all of this is easy. He said: “By the One in whose hand my soul is, there is no servant who acts on one of these traits, seeking by it what is with Allah, but it will take him by the hand on the Day of Resurrection until he enters Paradise.”

So in this hadith he made sincerity of intention a condition for all of these deeds, as in the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr which mentions the forty traits. This is like His words, the Mighty and Majestic:

“There is no good in much of their private conversation, except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or setting things right between people; and whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah — We shall give him a great reward” [al-Nisāʾ 4:114].
It has been narrated from al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn that one is rewarded for doing good even if one has no intention in it.
Al-Ḥasan was asked about a man whom someone he dislikes asks for something he needs, and who gives it to him out of shyness: does he have a reward for it?
He said: That is part of doing good, and in doing good there is a reward.
Ḥumayd ibn Zanjawayh recorded it.
Ibn Sīrīn was asked about a man who follows a funeral procession, not seeking the reward but out of shyness before the family of the deceased: does he have a reward for that?
He said: One reward?
No, he has two rewards: a reward for praying over his brother, and a reward for keeping ties with the living.
Abū Nuʿaym recorded it in al-Ḥilyah.
Among the kinds of charity is fulfilling the rights a Muslim has over another Muslim, some of which are mentioned in the preceding hadiths. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said:

“The rights of a Muslim over a Muslim are five: returning the greeting, visiting the sick, following funerals, accepting invitations and blessing one who sneezes.” In a narration of Muslim's: “A Muslim has six rights over a Muslim.” Someone said: What are they, Messenger of Allah?

He said: “When you meet him, greet him; when he invites you, accept; when he asks your counsel, give him sincere counsel; when he sneezes and praises Allah, bless him; when he falls ill, visit him; and when he dies, follow [his funeral].”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from al-Barāʾ, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded us to do seven things: to visit the sick, follow the funeral, bless one who sneezes, help others fulfil their oaths, help the wronged, accept the invitation of one who invites, and spread the greeting of peace.
In a narration of Muslim's, “guiding one who has lost his way” takes the place of helping others fulfil their oaths.
Among the kinds of charity is walking to deliver to people the rights that are due to them. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Whoever walks to his brother with his due in order to pay it has a charity for every step.
Among them is granting respite to one in hardship. In the Musnad and the Sunan of Ibn Mājah, from Buraydah as marfūʿ:

“Whoever grants respite to one in hardship has a charity for every day before the debt falls due; and when the debt falls due and he grants him respite after that, he has for every day the like of it in charity.”

Among them is kindness to animals, as the Prophet ﷺ said when he was asked about giving them water: “In every moist liver there is a reward.” He also told of a prostitute who gave water to a dog panting with thirst, and she was forgiven.

As for charity whose benefit is confined to the one who does it, examples are the forms of remembrance — tasbīḥ, takbīr, taḥmīd, tahlīl and seeking forgiveness — and invoking blessings on the Prophet ﷺ; likewise reciting the Qurʾān, walking to the mosques, and sitting in them to wait for the prayer or to listen to remembrance.
Among them also are humility in dress, gait and bearing; dressing plainly for work; and earning what is lawful, taking care that it is so.

Among them too are calling oneself to account for one's past deeds; remorse and repentance for past sins, and grief over them; holding oneself in low esteem, disparaging oneself and detesting oneself for the sake of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; and weeping out of fear of Allah the Exalted;

and reflecting on the dominion of the heavens and the earth, on the matters of the Hereafter and the promise and threat they hold, and the like, which increases faith in the heart and gives rise to many of the deeds of the heart, such as fear, love, hope, reliance on Allah and others.

It has been said that this reflection is better than voluntary bodily deeds. This was narrated from more than one of the Successors, among them Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, al-Ḥasan and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and there is something in the words of Imam Aḥmad that indicates it.
Kaʿb said: To weep out of fear of Allah is dearer to me than to give my weight in gold in charity.
